sources.locator: GNU C Language Introduction and Reference Manual; accessed 2026-07; provisions applicable to if and switch
sources.claim: C selection uses scalar conditions where zero is false and nonzero is true, with if/else binding and switch case labels determining one control path.

canonicalExplanation.summary: In C, a condition is any scalar value: **0 is false, anything else is true**. `if / else if / else` checks conditions top to bottom and runs **exactly one** branch. An `else` pairs with the **nearest unmatched `if`**, so use braces to make pairing obvious. `switch` jumps to the matching `case` label for an integer value, then **keeps running into the next cases** (fall-through) until a `break`. Always add `break` (or a comment saying fall-through is deliberate) and a `default`. Test every **boundary**: the values just below, at and above each dividing line.

sections.heading: Start here
sections.body:
A learner writes a menu with switch: choosing option 1 prints "Add", "Delete" and "Quit" all at once. Separately, their sign checker says 0 is positive. An if/else-if chain handles negative, zero, and positive values in mutually exclusive branches and tests both boundaries. In this lesson you'll implement and test boundary-complete if and switch logic.

includes: Write mutually exclusive if/else-if chains and switch statements with break and default.
Test values below, at and above every boundary.
excludes: Switching on strings (not possible in C).

outcomes: Implement and test boundary-complete if and switch logic.

examples.title: Negative, zero or positive
examples.situation: An if/else-if chain handles negative, zero, and positive values in mutually exclusive branches and tests both boundaries.
walkthrough: **An if/else-if chain:** n < 0, then n == 0, then else.
**Handles negative, zero, and positive values in mutually exclusive branches:** exactly one return runs.
**Tests both boundaries:** sign(-1), sign(0) and sign(1) will return negative, zero and positive.
examples.result: Zero is no longer called positive, and the tests prove every branch.

examples.title: The menu that did everything
examples.situation: Option 1 printed Add, Delete and Quit because no case had break.
walkthrough: Execution jumped to case 1, then fell through cases 2 and 3.
Add break after each case's statements.
Add default for invalid options, and test 1, 2, 3 and 4.
examples.result: Each option does exactly one thing.

misconceptions.mistakenBelief: Every switch case stops automatically when its statements finish, even without break or another control transfer.
misconceptions.correction: C falls through into the next case unless break, return or another jump stops it. Add break to each case and mark deliberate fall-through.
misconceptions.diagnosticPrompt: In "The menu that did everything", why did option 1 print three words?

analogy.example: An if/else-if chain is **a row of doors where you take the first one that opens**. A switch is **a lift that stops at your floor, but without a break it keeps going down through every floor below** until something stops it.
limitations: Lifts go one way; C falls through only downwards in the code.
default is the ground floor for unknown requests.

steps.explanation: The chain handles negative values in the first branch.
Zero takes its own mutually exclusive branch.
Positive values fall to else, so both boundaries are tested.

trace.textAlternative: Tracing boundary tests. Step 1, Below: n is -1; branch is n < 0. The chain handles negative values in the first branch. Step 2, At: n is 0; branch is n == 0. Zero takes its own mutually exclusive branch. Step 3, Above: n is 1; branch is else. Positive values fall to else, so both boundaries are tested.

nearTransfer.prompt: Write grade(int score) returning 'A' for 90 to 100, 'B' for 80 to 89, 'C' for 0 to 79, and '?' otherwise. Test 101, 100, 90, 89, 80, 79, 0 and -1.

farTransfer.prompt: Write a switch-based calculator for + - * / on two ints, with default for unknown operators and a guard for division by zero. Include one deliberate fall-through (for example 'x' and '*' both multiply) with a comment.

remediation.explanation: For every branch structure, list **the boundary values** and **which branch each should take**, then test them. For every case, check: **does it end with break or return?**
remediation.retryPrompt: Apply this to "The menu that did everything".

recap.summary: To implement boundary-complete selection, remember zero is false and nonzero true, order if/else-if conditions so exactly one branch runs, use braces to avoid dangling else, end each switch case with break (or a comment for deliberate fall-through) plus a default, and test below, at and above each boundary.
